title: Recognizing Opinions That Come From Fear and Insecurity
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article gives leaders a framework for weighting opinions unevenly rather than treating all input as equally valid, with particular attention to spotting opinions rooted in fear and insecurity rather than evidence. It identifies several telltale language cues: absolutist framing (always/never, good/bad), a preoccupation with image and status, heavy emphasis on rules and procedure, and language about getting in "trouble" or avoiding blame. The piece argues that fear-based opinions, while often the most emotionally persuasive, don't hold up under scrutiny and should be given proportionally less weight in decision-making, closing with the directive that when fear and facts collide, the facts must win.
points: Good leaders weight opinions unevenly, favoring those grounded in evidence, expertise, and skin in the outcome.
Opinions rooted in fear and insecurity are often the most emotionally persuasive but typically don't hold up under scrutiny.
Telltale signs of fear-based opinions include absolutist language, preoccupation with image/status, and heavy emphasis on rules and procedure.
When fear-based and fact-based views collide, the article argues the facts must be given more weight.
quotes: Some are grounded in facts and data, while others are situated in experience and intuition. Good leaders consider everyone’s opinions while forming their own.
good leaders are especially on guard about opinions that come from fear and insecurity .
While fearful opinions contain valuable insights about the risk and safety issues involved, they typically don’t hold up when interrogated for their reasoning and logic.
Fear-based opinions commonly incorporate absolutist language , such as always/never and good/bad, unsupported by proportional evidence.
But once judged to be grounded in fear, an opinion must be given less weight, or a leader stands the chance of forming an overly protective and cautious opinion.
